A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same MONA research. Their complete main texts, figures, tables, equations, and appendices support comparison. Retained appendix material can be matched despite renumbering and relocation.

before.justification: v1 reports original LLM experiments on Test-driven Development and Loan Applications, plus tabular and PPO experiments on Camera Dropbox, in Section 4 and Appendix D.

after.justification: v2 retains these original experiments and adds reported auction outcomes, transcript analyses, and a loan-decision coordination experiment in Appendices B, E, and F.1.

M1.justification: The MONA objective, myopic optimization, approval mechanism, M-step variant, and tabular and policy-gradient implementations remain unchanged. The implementation appendix moves from C.4 to D.4; the additional applications and diagnostic controls do not revise the proposed algorithm.

E1.justification: New Appendix B reports experiments with two agents competing in repeated auctions, including variants permitting communication. This extends coverage to coordination between distinct agents, beyond the retained coding, loan-decision, and gridworld tasks. The auction findings qualify as added coverage despite being inconclusive.

E2.justification: Appendix F.1 newly compares trained agents' loan decisions against a frozen Gemini 1.5 Flash decision maker using their summaries. v2 Figure 13 also adds ordinary RL to the reward-hacking initialization comparison, which showed only MONA in v1 Figure 12. The principal MONA-versus-ordinary-RL comparisons remain.

E3.justification: v2 adds a frozen-decision substitution protocol and learned decision advantage metric, and reports an experiment reversing the monitoring reward. The PPO figures replace behavior frequencies with observed and ground-truth returns and extend the displayed training duration from 300,000/200,000 steps to one million steps. Newly specified loan-data generation details do not establish changes to the original dataset.

E4.justification: New Appendix E examines coding and loan transcripts across training stages; Appendix F.1 tests dependence on learned coordination between loan-summary and decision steps. Section 4.2 adds the monitoring-reward sign-reversal observation. The existing PPO unlearning analysis gains an ordinary-RL control, while the no-approval, grid-size, and reward-hack-complexity analyses are retained.

E5.justification: The main appendix PPO comparison changes from displaying the best of three trials in v1 Figure 11 to reporting averages of ten trials per method in v2 Figure 12. Main-text LLM seed reporting is unchanged. v2 Figure 13 retains the best-of-three caption despite showing multiple curves, leaving its aggregation unclear.

E6.justification: Added findings include unsuccessful sustained auction coordination, qualitatively unchanged loan behavior after reversing the monitor reward, and learned decision advantage around 50% for MONA while ordinary RL starts lower and rises during training. Transcript observations and replacement PPO return curves further expand the results. The main plots remain unchanged; the revised PPO plots do not establish a same-setting performance improvement.

T1.justification: The original theorems, proofs, and nonmonotonic-horizon counterexample are unchanged after Appendix B becomes C. A limited mathematical addition is the learned decision advantage definition in F.1/Figure 10: the reward difference from a frozen decision maker, normalized by the agent's reward in the caption. The prose omits that normalization.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's contribution list, and conclusion retain the same claims about mitigating multi-step reward hacking through myopic optimization and non-myopic approval. The performance tradeoff and inability to solve single-step reward hacking remain unchanged.

C2.justification: v2 substantially expands mechanism interpretation: ordinary RL is interpreted as progressing from coordination-free to coordinated loan reward hacking; monitoring-reward insensitivity is attributed tentatively to the model's pre-existing avoidance of nationality mentions. Appendix E links trivial coding solutions to the length penalty, while Appendix B discusses learning difficulties as a possible explanation for unsuccessful auction coordination.

D1.justification: v2 adds stated access to Camera Dropbox source code and full experiment transcripts. Appendix D.2.1 newly specifies loan-data sampling ranges, categorical values, expense noise with standard deviation 10% of income, nationality-label mapping, and the application template. These substantially expand reproduction information, although proprietary LLM training details remain undisclosed and the linked resources were not inspected.

R1.justification: Section 5 and the bibliography are unchanged after accounting for wrapping. The positioning relative to approval-directed agents, decoupled approval, process supervision, and prior steganography research is retained.

P1.justification: v2 makes localized wording corrections, replaces leftover TFO terminology with MONA, subdivides loan-task documentation, and introduces appendix sections for auctions, transcripts, and coordination analysis. Existing appendices are renumbered, but the main narrative and section sequence remain largely unchanged.

P2.justification: v2 adds the loan-coordination Figure 10 and redesigns the PPO and unlearning displays as return curves in Figures 12–13. Retained appendix figures are relocated and renumbered; main figures and table designs remain stable. Figure 13's caption still incorrectly describes a behavior-distribution plot.

improvement.justification: v2 improves empirical scrutiny through the coordination control, transcript analysis, and disclosure of inconclusive auctions. Replacing a selected PPO trial with ten-trial averages and expanding reproduction information also strengthen the paper. These gains are limited but clear; inconsistencies in the new diagnostic's normalization and Figure 13's outdated caption reduce reporting clarity without outweighing the benefits.
